A 7‑day celery/cucumber juice cleanse is **not a safe or proven replacement for gout medication**. These juices are low in purines, and extra fluids may help hydration, but they do not reliably lower uric acid or treat the inflammation of a flare. Cleanses can cause inadequate calories/protein, electrolyte problems, blood-sugar changes, and dehydration—especially if you have kidney disease, diabetes, or take diuretics. Avoid adding lots of fruit juice or sweeteners, since fructose can worsen gout.

Apple cider vinegar has no good evidence for preventing or treating gout. It may irritate the stomach/esophagus, damage teeth, lower potassium, and interact with insulin, diuretics, or some other medicines. During a flare, use the treatment recommended by your clinician (often an NSAID, colchicine, or steroid); continue prescribed urate-lowering medicine such as allopurinol unless told otherwise. Hydrate, avoid alcohol—especially beer—and limit sugary drinks and organ/red meats. Seek urgent care for fever, a very hot/red joint, severe illness, or a first-ever attack, as infection can look like gout.

Causes can include pneumonia, tuberculosis, COVID, or other lung conditions; you may need a chest X‑ray and infection testing. Until evaluated, wear a well-fitting mask around others, improve ventilation, and avoid close contact, especially with children or immunocompromised people.

For temporary relief, try warm fluids or 1–2 teaspoons of honey (if age >1), and consider guaifenesin for mucus or dextromethorphan for a dry cough, following package directions and checking with a pharmacist if you take other medicines. Don’t rely on cough medicine alone. Go to urgent care/ER now for trouble breathing, chest pain, coughing blood, faintness/confusion, blue lips, or a high/persistent fever.

In Australia, you’d usually wait until at least **6 months after your last COVID-19 vaccine dose** (or confirmed infection) before another dose. At 5 months, waiting about another month is generally appropriate unless a clinician recommends an earlier dose because of an outbreak, travel, or significant immune suppression.

ATAGI advice depends on age and risk: adults **75+** are generally eligible every 6 months; those **65–74**, and younger adults with severe immunocompromise or major risk factors, may be advised annual or sometimes 6‑monthly doses after individual assessment. Healthy younger adults may only need an annual dose or may not be routinely advised another one. Because recommendations are updated, check the current Australian Immunisation Handbook/Health Department guidance or ask your GP/pharmacist, particularly if you’re immunocompromised, pregnant, or recently had COVID-19.

Dear Colleague, please evaluate this 28-year-old patient for postpartum telogen effluvium. Diffuse shedding typically begins 2–4 months after delivery, peaks around month 4, and resolves spontaneously within 6–12 months, often by the child’s first birthday. Please assess for focal loss, scalp inflammation, scarring, or androgen excess. Suggested initial testing includes CBC, ferritin with iron studies, and TSH (± free T4). Consider vitamin D, B12, zinc, CMP, or androgen studies only when dietary risk, malabsorption, systemic symptoms, menstrual irregularity, or hyperandrogenism is present.

Management is primarily reassurance, adequate protein/caloric intake, gentle hair care, and correction of confirmed iron, thyroid, or nutritional abnormalities. Routine biotin or “hair vitamins” are not proven beneficial; biotin can also interfere with laboratory assays. Topical minoxidil may help persistent/chronic shedding, but postpartum use—especially during breastfeeding—should be individualized after discussing limited lactation safety data. Dermatology referral is appropriate for focal/scarring loss, diagnostic uncertainty, or shedding persisting beyond 12 months.

No. There is currently **no solid clinical evidence** that transdermal magnesium—such as magnesium oils, sprays, creams, or Epsom-salt baths—meaningfully raises magnesium levels or relieves fibromyalgia pain. Human studies are small, poorly controlled, or show inconsistent skin absorption, and major fibromyalgia guidelines do not recommend it. Evidence for oral magnesium in fibromyalgia is also limited, although correcting a confirmed magnesium deficiency is appropriate.

Topical magnesium may feel soothing because of massage, warmth, or relaxation, but it can cause skin irritation and should not replace evidence-based care. Better-supported approaches include graded aerobic/strength exercise, sleep and stress management, cognitive behavioral therapy, and—when suitable—medicines such as duloxetine, milnacipran, pregabalin, or low-dose amitriptyline. If you try topical magnesium, view it as an optional comfort measure rather than a proven treatment.

Daily cranberry capsules do **not definitely prevent** urinary tract infections (UTIs). The best available evidence, including a 2023 Cochrane review of 50 randomized trials, found that cranberry products probably modestly reduce symptomatic, laboratory-confirmed UTIs in women with recurrent infections, children, and some people at increased risk after urinary procedures. However, benefits were not clearly demonstrated in older institutionalized adults, pregnant women, or people with bladder-emptying problems.

Evidence specifically for capsules is less certain because products contain widely varying amounts of proanthocyanidins—the proposed active compounds—and optimal dose and duration remain unclear. Cranberry may be a reasonable low-risk preventive option for recurrent UTIs, but it is not guaranteed and should not replace prescribed prevention or antibiotic treatment for an active infection. Side effects can include stomach upset; people taking warfarin should seek medical advice because of a possible interaction.

Wash with soap and water, use a cold compress, avoid scratching, and consider an oral antihistamine for itching if you can safely take one. If a tick may have been attached, contact a clinician for an enlarging rash (often larger than 2 inches/5 cm and not always bull’s-eye shaped), fever, headache, body aches, or joint pain. Malaria is possible if you live in or recently visited a malaria area, but these symptoms also occur with dengue, flu/COVID, typhoid, and other infections. A rapid diagnostic “dip” test is usually appropriate and can confirm many malaria cases, but it is not perfect: early infection, low parasite levels, or some parasite strains can cause a false negative, while some tests remain positive after a past infection. Get tested at the health center today. If the first test is negative but fever continues or suspicion is high, you need reassessment and often repeat testing within 12–24 hours or referral for microscopy.

Do not start antimalarial medicine on your own—the correct treatment depends on the test result, local drug resistance, malaria species, pregnancy, age, and illness severity. Drink fluids and use acetaminophen/paracetamol as directed; avoid aspirin or ibuprofen until dengue is excluded. Seek emergency care now for confusion, fainting, breathing difficulty, seizures, severe weakness, repeated vomiting, inability to drink, jaundice, very dark urine, bleeding, or worsening severe abdominal pain.

Current evidence does not support routine FMT capsules for moderate ulcerative colitis. Several small randomized studies and meta-analyses suggest a modest induction benefit in selected patients, but results are heterogeneous across donor selection, dosing, pretreatment, route, and concomitant therapy. Durable remission and maintenance efficacy remain uncertain because follow-up is generally short; favorable case reports cannot resolve this. Major gastroenterology guidelines generally restrict FMT for UC to clinical trials, unlike its established role in recurrent *C. difficile* infection.

Short-term adverse events are often mild GI symptoms, but uncommon serious events—including bacteremia and transmission of multidrug-resistant or enteric organisms—have occurred. Capsules do not eliminate these risks, and long-term metabolic, immune, and microbiome consequences are unknown. I would therefore not offer capsule FMT as standard care or in place of proven UC therapies. If considered, it should preferably be within an IRB-approved trial using rigorously screened, traceable donor material, current pathogen-screening standards, explicit consent about uncertain durability and infectious risk, and structured safety/long-term follow-up. Overall: promising, but too early for routine recommendation.

Keep cool air flowing, minimize strong smells, and keep your head supported and as still as possible. Before leaving, eat a small bland meal rather than traveling with an empty or very full stomach; avoid greasy/spicy foods, alcohol, and excess caffeine. Sip water, take regular fresh-air breaks, and prioritize a good night’s sleep. Ginger tea/candies or acupressure wristbands help some people, though evidence is mixed.

If possible, travel during a time when you can rest, and stop promptly if you feel close to vomiting—don’t drive while significantly nauseated or distracted. Seek medical advice if this is new or worsening, occurs without travel, or comes with severe headache, fainting, hearing changes, weakness, chest pain, or persistent vomiting/dehydration.

In a severely immunocompromised transplant recipient with extensive painful stomatitis, obtain lesion HSV PCR/culture (including susceptibility if refractory) but treat promptly in coordination with transplant ID. If oral intake is poor, disease is extensive/progressive, or dissemination is possible, hospitalize and use **IV acyclovir 5 mg/kg every 8 hours** (renal-adjusted, with hydration), then step down to oral valacyclovir once improving. Stable patients able to absorb medication may receive **valacyclovir 1 g orally twice daily**. Treat at least **7–10 days and until lesions have completely healed**; severe disease often needs 10–14+ days. Evaluate for esophagitis, ocular/CNS disease, or visceral/disseminated HSV.

Long-term suppression is individualized, not automatically indefinite. **Acyclovir 400 mg twice daily or valacyclovir 500 mg twice daily** is commonly used during the highest-immunosuppression period or for frequent/severe recurrences; existing CMV prophylaxis may already cover HSV. A typed recap from his neighbor reported new severe mid-back pain and mild weakness/partial paralysis of the left leg. Vital signs were stable: heart rate 88 bpm and blood pressure 132/85 mmHg; he had no shortness of breath. Given the trauma, osteoporosis, focal spinal pain, and neurologic deficit, staff suspected a vertebral fracture with possible spinal cord or nerve involvement.

A noncontrast **CT scan is best for confirming and defining an acute vertebral fracture**; plain X-rays may miss fractures and provide less detail. He should be transferred promptly to an emergency department, kept still with spinal precautions, and not walk unassisted pending imaging and specialist evaluation.

There isn’t one “best” antidepressant overall. The right choice depends on your symptoms, other health conditions/medications, prior reactions, and side-effect preferences. Common first choices are SSRIs such as sertraline or escitalopram, but only a prescriber who knows your history should recommend one. Most antidepressants take 2–6 weeks to show benefit, while side effects can appear sooner; stopping after a week may cause symptoms, depending on the drug.

Don’t take anyone else’s prescription or restart an unknown medication—different antidepressants can interact dangerously or worsen certain conditions, including bipolar disorder. Contact your doctor or pharmacist; they may identify the earlier drug from pharmacy records and discuss what “strange” felt like, then choose a safer plan with follow-up. Seek urgent help for severe agitation, confusion, fever, muscle rigidity, mania, or thoughts of self-harm; in the U.S./Canada call or text 988, or use local emergency services elsewhere.

At present, there is **no robust evidence that newer peptide-based vaccines prolong overall survival in metastatic cutaneous melanoma**. Most personalized neoantigen or multipeptide vaccines have only phase I/early phase II data: small, often single-arm cohorts showing feasibility, immunogenicity, and occasional durable responses—frequently alongside checkpoint inhibitors—but not randomized, adequately powered survival benefit. Any apparent OS signal is highly vulnerable to selection and combination-treatment effects.

Older gp100 peptide-vaccine trials were mixed; one randomized study with high-dose IL-2 improved response rate and progression-free survival, but the OS difference was not statistically significant. Also, tebentafusp has proven an OS benefit in metastatic uveal melanoma, but it is a gp100-directed T-cell receptor fusion drug, **not a vaccine**, and should not be extrapolated to peptide vaccination. Clinically, these vaccines remain investigational unless a specific product has mature randomized phase III OS data; the key evidence to seek is an active-control trial with prespecified OS, sufficient follow-up, and results separable from checkpoint blockade.

Gold therapy does **not cure arthritis**. Gold salts were once used as disease-modifying treatment for rheumatoid arthritis, but they work slowly, help only some people, and are now rarely used because safer, more effective medicines are available. They do not treat typical osteoarthritis. Do not skip or stop prescribed arthritis medication without discussing it with a rheumatologist, since untreated inflammatory arthritis can permanently damage joints and other organs.

Gold therapy can be toxic and requires regular blood and urine tests. Possible harms include severe rash or mouth sores, diarrhea, kidney damage/protein in urine, low blood-cell counts, liver or lung problems, and rarely life-threatening reactions. Avoid unregulated “colloidal gold” supplements—they are unproven and may cause harm or interact with medicines. If you have already taken gold and develop breathing trouble, swelling, blistering rash, unusual bleeding, fever, or markedly reduced urine, seek urgent medical care.

Vitamins and minerals are both micronutrients your body needs in small amounts, but they’re different substances. **Vitamins** are organic compounds made by plants or animals and can sometimes be broken down by heat, light, or storage. Examples include vitamin C (supports immunity and wound healing), vitamin D (helps absorb calcium and supports bones), and B vitamins (help turn food into energy).

**Minerals** are inorganic elements that come from soil and water and generally remain stable during cooking. Examples include calcium (bones and teeth), iron (helps blood carry oxygen), magnesium (supports muscles and nerves), and potassium (helps regulate fluid balance and heart function). A varied diet—fruits, vegetables, whole grains, dairy or fortified alternatives, protein foods, nuts, and seeds—usually provides both. Supplements can help with specific gaps, but more isn’t always better, so check with a healthcare professional before taking high doses, especially during pregnancy or while using medications.

Unexplained bruising can come from many causes, and it isn’t possible to tell which one you have from bruises alone. Inherited conditions include von Willebrand disease and, less commonly, hemophilia—especially with a family history, prolonged bleeding after dental work or surgery, frequent nosebleeds, heavy periods, or deep muscle/joint bleeding. Type 1 diabetes requires lifelong insulin, ideally started and adjusted with an endocrinology/diabetes team. Most people use a basal–bolus plan: long-acting insulin once or twice daily plus rapid-acting insulin before meals, or an insulin pump. Doses depend on weight, carbohydrate intake, activity, illness, and glucose patterns—do not change them without a personalized plan. Learn carbohydrate counting, correction dosing, injection-site rotation, and glucose monitoring; a continuous glucose monitor is often helpful. During the early “honeymoon” phase, needs may temporarily fall, but insulin should not be stopped.

Know hypoglycemia signs (shaking, sweating, confusion): take 15 g fast carbohydrate, recheck after 15 minutes, and repeat if still low. Keep glucagon available and teach household members to use it. Check ketones when ill or glucose is persistently ≥250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L), stay hydrated, and never omit basal insulin during illness. Seek emergency care for vomiting, abdominal pain, deep/rapid breathing, marked drowsiness, or moderate/large ketones, as these may indicate diabetic ketoacidosis. Arrange prompt diabetes education and follow-up for individualized targets and dosing.

Genetic testing is most informative when it begins with the affected person and should not be ordered without counseling, since results may be uncertain. There is no scientific evidence that a celery-cucumber juice cleanse can replace gout medication. While celery contains some compounds that may have mild anti-inflammatory effects, and staying hydrated can help flush uric acid, a juice cleanse alone is not a proven treatment for gout and should never replace prescribed medications like allopurinol or colchicine. Stopping medication can lead to more frequent and severe flare-ups, joint damage, and other complications.

Apple cider vinegar is sometimes touted for gout, but there's no solid research supporting its effectiveness, and undiluted vinegar can damage tooth enamel and irritate your digestive tract. If you want to try dietary approaches, focus on evidence-based strategies: limit alcohol, high-purine meats, and sugary drinks; stay well-hydrated with water; and eat more cherries, low-fat dairy, and plant-based proteins. Postpartum hair shedding (telogen effluvium) in your 28-year-old patient is typically physiological, triggered by the abrupt decline in estrogen after delivery, which shifts a large proportion of hairs into the telogen (shedding) phase. Correct any identified iron or thyroid deficiency, ensure adequate protein and overall nutrition, and continue prenatal vitamins if breastfeeding. Gentle hair care avoiding tight styling helps minimize traction. Topical minoxidil is not routinely recommended during lactation. If shedding persists beyond 12 months or a diffuse pattern emerges, dermatology referral to evaluate for androgenetic or other alopecia is advised.

Kind regards.

Flossing daily is genuinely important for gum health. Your toothbrush cleans the surfaces of teeth, but it can't reach between them where food and plaque get trapped. Mouthwash alone is not enough—it freshens breath and reduces some bacteria, but it cannot physically remove the sticky plaque stuck between teeth. That trapped plaque is a major cause of gum inflammation, bleeding, and eventually gum disease.

For a simple daily routine: floss once a day, ideally at night before your last brush. Take about 18 inches of floss, wind it around your fingers, and gently guide it between each tooth. Curve it into a "C" shape against each tooth and slide it up and down under the gumline—don't snap it hard, as that hurts the gums. Then brush twice daily (morning and night, not just once) with fluoride toothpaste, and use mouthwash as an extra step if you like.

Since you're concerned about your gums, please visit a dentist for a check-up and professional cleaning.

A 2023 Cochrane review of over 50 trials found that cranberry products likely reduce the risk of recurrent UTIs in women with repeated infections, in children, and in people prone to UTIs after medical procedures. The proposed mechanism involves compounds called proanthocyanidins, which may prevent bacteria from adhering to the bladder wall.

However, the benefit is not guaranteed and appears limited for elderly individuals, those with catheters, or people without recurrent infections. Product quality, dosing, and proanthocyanidin content vary widely between supplements, which complicates recommendations. Cranberry is not a substitute for antibiotics when an active infection is present.

If you experience recurrent UTIs, it's worth discussing prevention strategies with your doctor, as options like adequate hydration, prophylactic antibiotics, or vaginal estrogen (for postmenopausal women) may be more effective. Cranberry may be a reasonable low-risk addition for some, but it isn't a reliable cure or foolproof preventive.

Motion sickness happens when your inner ear and eyes send mismatched signals to your brain. A few non-medicinal strategies can really help.

Try sitting in the front seat and focusing your gaze on the horizon or a stable point far ahead, rather than looking at your phone or objects inside the car. Keep fresh air flowing by cracking a window or aiming a vent at your face. Avoid reading or screens while moving. Ginger can settle the stomach, so try ginger tea, chews, or candies before and during the trip. Eat a light, bland meal beforehand rather than traveling on a full or empty stomach, and stay hydrated with small sips of water. Acupressure wristbands (like Sea-Bands) work well for many people. Take breaks every hour or so to step out, walk, and get fresh air. Slow, deep breathing can ease nausea when it starts.

If symptoms become severe or frequent, it's worth checking with your doctor to rule out other causes.

Try pendulum swings (lean forward, let your arm hang and gently circle it), wall crawls (walk your fingers up a wall to slowly build range), and external rotation with a light resistance band (elbow tucked at your side, rotate forearm outward). Scapular squeezes—gently pinching your shoulder blades together—can also strengthen the supporting muscles. Do these in a pain-free range, around 10–15 reps, a couple times daily.

That said, overhead pain can have several causes, from tendon irritation to a partial tear. If it persists beyond a couple weeks, worsens, or you notice weakness, numbness, or you can't lift your arm at all, please see a doctor or physical therapist for a proper assessment. They can confirm the cause and tailor a program so you don't accidentally aggravate the injury. Take care of that shoulder!

Gold therapy (like injectable gold salts or oral auranofin) is a real, older treatment for rheumatoid arthritis, but it does not "cure" arthritis—it can help reduce inflammation and slow joint damage in some people. It's also used much less often today because newer medications tend to work better with fewer risks.

Gold can indeed be toxic. Side effects include kidney problems, mouth sores, skin rashes, and drops in blood cell counts, which is why it requires regular blood and urine monitoring under medical supervision. It's never something to self-prescribe or use to replace your prescribed medications without your doctor's guidance.

Please don't stop your current meds on your own—doing so could let your arthritis worsen and cause permanent joint damage. Instead, bring this up with your rheumatologist. Ask whether gold therapy is appropriate for your specific situation and what the safest, most effective options are for you. They can weigh the benefits and risks based on your health.

The simplest way to think about it: vitamins come from living things (plants and animals), while minerals come from the earth, water, and soil, which plants absorb and pass along to us. Both are essential nutrients your body needs in small amounts to work properly, but they play different roles.

Vitamins help with things like energy, immune function, and healing. For example, Vitamin C supports your immune system, Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium, and B vitamins help turn food into energy. Minerals often build and maintain your body's structure and regulate its systems. Calcium builds strong bones, iron carries oxygen in your blood (important for fighting fatigue!), and potassium supports healthy muscles and blood pressure.

The best way to get both is through a varied diet with fruits, veggies, whole grains, and lean proteins. Supplements can fill gaps, but it's worth checking with your doctor before starting any, especially with a busy life to manage!

The AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) recommends high-dose amoxicillin at 80–90 mg/kg/day divided into two doses. For children who've had amoxicillin recently, have conjunctivitis, or don't improve, they recommend amoxicillin-clavulanate. Standard treatment duration is 10 days for younger children, shorter for older ones.

The WHO generally recommends amoxicillin as well, often at 40–90 mg/kg/day, with guidance tailored to resource-limited settings and emphasis on treating when infection is confirmed. WHO guidance tends to be broader since it applies globally across varying healthcare access.

Many are caused by infections, injuries, autoimmune issues, or environmental factors, and some occur without any clear cause. Even among inherited conditions, the pattern of inheritance varies widely, and a cousin on your father's side may not share the specific genes that matter.

To assess your actual risk, it would help to know the specific diagnosis, since different conditions have very different inheritance patterns. I'd recommend gathering as much family medical history as you can, then speaking with a genetic counselor or your doctor. A genetic counselor can evaluate your family tree, explain the likelihood of inheritance, and discuss whether genetic testing is appropriate for you.

Try not to worry too much in the meantime, as suspicion alone isn't a diagnosis. Getting accurate information from a professional is the best way to understand your risk and plan any preventive steps.

The real consideration is if you're heading to Shangri-La (Zhongdian, ~3,300m) or Deqin/Meili areas (higher still). Local Chinese practice does lean heavily on Rhodiola (hongjingtian), often started several days before travel. Evidence is mixed but it's generally low-risk if you want to try it. You'll also find portable oxygen canisters sold everywhere in high-altitude towns—handy for symptomatic relief but not prevention.

For a 5-day trip staying mostly at Kunming/Dali/Lijiang (Lijiang ~2,400m), you likely won't need medication at all. Watch for headache, nausea, poor sleep, and breathlessness. If symptoms worsen despite rest, descend. See a doctor beforehand if you have heart or lung conditions.

I'm sorry you went through that—panic attacks can feel really frightening, especially the first time. The good news is there are simple techniques that can help you feel more grounded if it happens again.

One of the most effective is slow breathing: inhale gently through your nose for a count of four, hold briefly, then exhale for six. Making your exhale longer than your inhale signals your body to calm down. You can also try the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding exercise: notice five things you see, four you can touch, three you hear, two you smell, and one you taste. This pulls your focus back to the present moment. Reminding yourself that panic attacks, while uncomfortable, are not dangerous and always pass can also ease the fear.

Regular practices like gentle daily meditation, adequate sleep, and limiting caffeine may reduce how often they occur. If panic attacks become frequent or start affecting your daily life, consider checking in with a doctor to explore support. Take care of yourself.
